#Text=It was high noon before we were got to Dulverton that day, near to which
#Text= town the river Exe and its big brother Barle have union.
#Text=My mother had
#Text= an uncle living there, but we were not to visit his house this time, at
#Text= which I was somewhat astonished, since we needs must stop for at least
#Text= two hours, to bait our horses thorough well, before coming to the black
#Text= bogway.
#Text=The bogs are very good in frost, except where the hot-springs
#Text= rise; but as yet there had been no frost this year, save just enough
#Text= to make the blackbirds look big in the morning.
#Text=In a hearty black-frost
#Text= they look small, until the snow falls over them.
#Text=The road from Bampton to Dulverton had not been very delicate, yet
#Text= nothing to complain of much--no deeper, indeed, than the hocks of a
#Text= horse, except in the rotten places.
#Text=The day was inclined to be mild and
#Text= foggy, and both nags sweated freely; but Peggy carrying little weight
#Text= (for my wardrobe was upon Smiler, and John Fry grumbling always), we
#Text= could easily keep in front, as far as you may hear a laugh.
#Text=John had been rather bitter with me, which methought was a mark of ill
#Text= taste at coming home for the holidays; and yet I made allowance for
#Text=John, because he had never been at school, and never would have chance
#Text= to eat fry upon condition of spelling it; therefore I rode on, thinking
#Text= that he was hard-set, like a saw, for his dinner, and would soften after
#Text= tooth-work.
#Text=And yet at his most hungry times, when his mind was far gone
#Text= upon bacon, certes he seemed to check himself and look at me as if he
#Text= were sorry for little things coming over great.
#Text=But now, at Dulverton, we dined upon the rarest and choicest victuals
#Text= that ever I did taste.
#Text=Even now, at my time of life, to think of it
#Text= gives me appetite, as once and awhile to think of my first love makes
#Text= me love all goodness.
#Text=Hot mutton pasty was a thing I had often heard
#Text= of from very wealthy boys and men, who made a dessert of dinner; and to
#Text= hear them talk of it made my lips smack, and my ribs come inwards.
#Text=And now John Fry strode into the hostel, with the air and grace of a
#Text= short-legged man, and shouted as loud as if he was calling sheep upon
#Text= Exmoor,--

#Text= When I came to myself again, my hands were full of
#Text= young grass and mould, and a little girl kneeling at my side was rubbing
#Text= my forehead tenderly with a dock-leaf and a handkerchief.
#Text="Oh, I am so glad," she whispered softly, as I opened my eyes and looked
#Text= at her; "now you will try to be better, won  '  t you?"
#Text=I had never heard so sweet a sound as came from between her bright red
#Text= lips, while there she knelt and gazed at me; neither had I ever seen
#Text= anything so beautiful as the large dark eyes intent upon me, full of
#Text= pity and wonder.
#Text=And then, my nature being slow, and perhaps, for that
#Text= matter, heavy, I wandered with my hazy eyes down the black shower of
#Text= her hair, as to my jaded gaze it seemed; and where it fell on the turf,
#Text= among it (like an early star) was the first primrose of the season.
#Text=And
#Text= since that day I think of her, through all the rough storms of my life,
#Text= when I see an early primrose.

#Text= Through that season of bitter frost the red deer of the forest, having
#Text= nothing to feed upon, and no shelter to rest in, had grown accustomed to
#Text= our ricks of corn, and hay, and clover.
#Text=There we might see a hundred
#Text= of them almost any morning, come for warmth, and food, and comfort, and
#Text= scarce willing to move away.
#Text=And many of them were so tame, that they
#Text= quietly presented themselves at our back door, and stood there with
#Text= their coats quite stiff, and their flanks drawn in and panting,
#Text= and icicles sometimes on their chins, and their great eyes fastened
#Text= wistfully upon any merciful person; craving for a bit of food, and a
#Text= drink of water; I suppose that they had not sense enough to chew the
#Text= snow and melt it; at any rate, all the springs being frozen, and rivers
#Text= hidden out of sight, these poor things suffered even more from thirst
#Text=vessels, should be the first to begin to fill.
#Text=And so we always arranged
#Text= it.
#Text=Now, though our Annie was a graceful maid, and Lizzie a very learned
#Text= one, you should have seen how differently Lorna managed her dining; she
#Text= never took more than about a quarter of a mouthful at a time, and she
#Text= never appeared to be chewing that, although she must have done so.
#Text=Indeed, she appeared to dine as if it were a matter of no consequence,
#Text= and as if she could think of other things more than of her business.
#Text=All
#Text= this, and her own manner of eating, I described to Eliza once, when I
#Text= wanted to vex her for something very spiteful that she had said; and
#Text= I never succeeded so well before, for the girl was quite outrageous,
#Text= having her own perception of it, which made my observation ten times as
#Text= bitter to her.
#Text=And I am not sure but what she ceased to like poor Lorna
#Text= from that day; and if so, I was quite paid out, as I well deserved, for
#Text= my bit of satire.
#Text=For it strikes me that of all human dealings, satire is the very lowest,
#Text= and most mean and common.
#Text=It is the equivalent in words of what bullying
#Text= is in deeds; and no more bespeaks a clever man, than the other does a
#Text=wrong, this time.
#Text=Lorna, come with me, my darling."
